pr_title: feat: argument every of datetime.truncate can be expression

issue_context.title: allow expression as parameters for dt.truncate
issue_context.body:
### Description

Currently dt.truncate does not seem to accept expressions as parameters.

This reduces the usability if different groups require different intervals but you do not know what those intervals will be beforehand.
Right now we workaround by either

- splitting the workloads and processing each group separately
- use a nested when-then to test all options
Both require upfront knowledge of the interval.

Use case is I have time series from IoT-devices, each device has a different heartbeat (every minute, every 5 minutes, ...). Truncation on the timestamps is required to ensure clock alignment of the signals.

@wouter-in2facts: just to be sure, you're looking for something like this, yes?
```python
import polars as pl
dtm = datetime(2023,9,13,1,2,3,4000)

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "timestamp": [dtm, dtm, dtm],
    "every": ["1h","1m","1s"],
})
df.with_columns(
    truncated_ts = pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate(pl.col("every"))
)
# ┌─────────────────────────┬───────┬─────────────────────┐
# │ timestamp               ┆ every ┆ truncated_ts        │
# │ ---                     ┆ ---   ┆ ---                 │
# │ datetime[μs]            ┆ str   ┆ datetime[μs]        │
# ╞═════════════════════════╪═══════╪═════════════════════╡
# │ 2023-09-13 01:02:03.004 ┆ 1h    ┆ 2023-09-13 01:00:00 │
# │ 2023-09-13 01:02:03.004 ┆ 1m    ┆ 2023-09-13 01:02:00 │
# │ 2023-09-13 01:02:03.004 ┆ 1s    ┆ 2023-09-13 01:02:03 │
# └─────────────────────────┴───────┴─────────────────────┘
```

Yes, exactly, thanks!
*update* every would be a timedelta though, not a string as dt.truncate expects durations (although implicit conversion can be used as it is the case for many other functions using timedeltas)

> every would be a timedelta though, not a string as dt.truncate expects durations 

For `timedelta` every, we actually convert python `timedelta` to a polars duration **string** before do the compute. As for `expression every`, If it is allowed to be `pl.Duration` type, it can become a bit tricky (although it is not impossible) when implementing `truncate`. I tend to support `every` column of `pl.Utf8` type first, then find a way to support `Duration` type later.

review_comments:
The reason why this is special(i.e. not use `try_binary_elementwise_values` to propagate null value ):

If we use `try_binary_elementwise_values` here, it will call `func(&w, timestamp, tz, ambiguous)` whether `every` is `None` or `Some`. As for `None`, `every` may be filled with any value. But some values are not allowed by `func` (such as zero duration).
I'm not totally sure I follow sorry - any chance you could show a test case where this makes a difference please?

The key point is data corresponding to `null` values in the `arrow array` can store any value. If we have a null `every` value parsed to a zero duration.
 
It will reach this branch, and then throw an error. But it should be view as `null` actually.

https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/7f8cd7dbd6bc09a21a99c13020fbac8cfdd4aa90/crates/polars-time/src/windows/duration.rs#L457
`try_binary_elementwise_values` will apply `op` for all values regardless of `validities`. I'm try to find a test case for this.

I have constructed a test case match this.

Replaced by `try_binary_elementwise_values` and then run the following code:

```python 
df = pl.DataFrame(
        {
            "date": [
                None,
                datetime(2022, 11, 14),
                datetime(2022, 3, 20, 5, 7, 18),
            ],
            "every": ["1y", None, "1m"],
        }
    )
df.select(
       pl.col("date").dt.truncate(every=pl.col("every"), ambiguous="latest")
)
```

You will get:

```python
exceptions.ComputeError: duration cannot be zero
```

IIUC, we expect to get `[None, None, datetime(2022, 3, 20, 5, 7, 0)]`

thanks for explaining - agree with your expected output

do you know why `None` is parsed as zero-duration? independently of this PR, perhaps that should be changed?

There are no special requirements for slots with `null` values in `Arrow Columnar Format`.
```
Array slots which are null are not required to have a particular value; any “masked” memory can have any value and need not be zeroed, though implementations frequently choose to zero memory for null values.
```
(From https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html#null-count)

So I think any `Duration` parsed for `None` is expected.

As for this case, we can go deeper:

Our upstream `arrow2` will fill the null value with empty `str` for `Utf8Array`.

See the following code:
https://github.com/jorgecarleitao/arrow2/blob/7c93e358fc400bf3c0c0219c22eefc6b38fc2d12/src/array/utf8/mutable.rs#L529-L535

So, we have `Duration::parse("")`(IIUC, this is a zero duration) for `None` value. IMO, We cannot expect a null slot to be a certain expected value as any modification of its value, as long as the validity is not modified, is legal.

`try_binary_elementwise` is better anyway. You should only use `try_binary_elementwise_values` if your function is very, very cheap (cheaper than a branch mispredict) and not worth skipping nulls for. Anything to do with parsing is way too expensive anyway and we should skip nulls for.

> You should only use try_binary_elementwise_values if your function is very, very cheap (cheaper than a branch mispredict) and not worth skipping nulls for.

Yep, make sense, and agree with you that this `parsing` is expensive and should skip any nulls. This reminds me to carefully check the implementation of other functions for similar performance issues. ^^

I see, that's very clear - thanks both for explaining!
